finding.statement: Candidate households are scored against the colonial signature - children Mary (a hard bound, born by 1631), Richard (about 1630, compiled) and John Jr. (about 1633, compiled); a wife Mary married by about 1630 and living to 1661; a father born about 1598-1608 and gone from England 1637-41 - on a points rubric that rewards each named child present, each child's baptism within two or five years of expectation, and the preserved birth order Mary then Richard then John; that grades the mother token from Mary at full weight through the Margaret family as a substantial soft hit to Margery as partial; that rewards a father in the John family and a father's implied birth year inside the band; that rewards a last record falling 1635-41 in a parish whose burials are demonstrably covered; and that penalises a violated birth order, a demonstrably continuing English household, each additional child with a non-colonial forename, and - as an effective elimination - an English burial or probate for the head after 1641. Six rules govern its application. Mary's date is a primary bound and the other two are not. The Mary and Margaret forms are a weighted scale rather than a filter, and Molly and Polly stay excluded as anachronistic. The John family on the father axis includes an indexed Jone or Joan, which in these sets is a contracted or Latin Johannes rather than a woman. An undated role row is never scored as an in-window household until it has been dated on a second instrument. Peter, Isaac and Sarah are not scored against a candidate at all. And a non-John father is a flag rather than a verdict, since an indexer has already been shown to misread a capital H as G, so any household scoring six or more on the child signals alone has its father's forename checked against the image regardless of the index.

unit.title: Identity — method for a complete child inventory

incoming.explanation: Scoring operates on assembled households, not on catalogued rows.

outgoing.explanation: The catalogue can only carry provenance if the instruments are enumerated first.

finding.shortLabel: One row per record instance, and a household split is a hypothesis rather than a finding

sources.alignmentNote: The case that produced the discipline.
sources.locator: The Great Berkhamsted father-John run of 1597-1637, the worked example of a baptism run too long for one man

finding.statement: Two disciplines govern how records become households. The catalogue takes one row per record instance, not per child: the same baptism indexed by four providers is four rows, because the disagreements between them are themselves evidence. Names are recorded exactly as indexed, since normalising to 'Gurney' destroys the variant evidence this work repeatedly needs, and no row enters without its instrument code and query date. Household assembly is where the July 2026 rounds failed hardest: four households were split on plausibility arguments and each split was then treated as a finding, when a split is a hypothesis about record shape and record shape is exactly what is uncertain. A household is therefore a set of catalogued rows plus an explicit shape hypothesis, never a bare assertion. Where a baptism run is too long for one father, the alternatives are enumerated rather than chosen between - one man with two wives; a father and son; two unrelated same-name men in one parish; an index conflating two parishes; a mis-transcribed father forename in some rows - and the evidence that would discriminate is recorded and the shape held open until it exists. No probability is built on an unresolved shape; where a row rests on a split, it is labelled conditional on that shape.
